items.title: Willis's 'lads'
items.claim: Paul Willis's Learning to Labour (1977) studied working-class boys in a Midlands school. What did he argue they were doing through their counter-school culture?

options.text: Actively rejecting school in ways that prepared them for manual labour

items.reveal_title: Resistance that reproduced the very inequality it opposed
items.reveal:
Willis combined Marxist theory with ethnography to argue the 'lads' partially saw through school ideology but their rejection led them into the same factory jobs their fathers held.

The study influenced both education research and cultural studies.
items.why: Ethnographic fieldwork can reveal mechanisms of class reproduction invisible in statistics.

items.title: Bourdieu's forms of capital
items.claim: Pierre Bourdieu argued that economic, cultural and social capital interact to reproduce class. What did he mean by 'cultural capital'?

options.text: Embodied dispositions, qualifications, and familiarity with high-status culture

items.reveal_title: Knowledge, manners and credentials function as inheritable assets
items.reveal:
Bourdieu (1986) distinguished embodied (dispositions), objectified (cultural goods) and institutionalised (qualifications) forms.

Empirical work continues to show cultural-capital indicators predict educational outcomes net of income.
items.why: Cultural capital explains why income alone underestimates the inheritance of advantage.

items.title: UK household structure today
items.claim: What proportion of UK households in 2022 were single-person households according to the Office for National Statistics?
items.reveal_title: Roughly three in ten UK households are one person
items.reveal:
ONS data for 2022 reported around 30% of households contained a single person. The figure has risen steadily since the 1960s.

The 'standard' nuclear family is now a minority household type.
items.why: Demographic change reshapes assumptions built into policy and earlier sociological theory.
